title: Queen's Gambit Declined: when it goes wrong and how to repair it
outcomes: Explains in a sentence why the c8 bishop is the problem piece of the Orthodox Declined, and names two ways to repair it (trades then a central break; the b6 route to the long diagonal)
Counts attackers and defenders on the target of a break before playing it, and shows with the e5 and c5 breaks that a mistimed break loses a pawn
Names the two typical Black slips of the Exchange Variation (a defender leaving h7, the c5 break at the wrong moment) and the two White slips (an h-pawn lunge without a target, the greedy pawn grab)
Diagnoses an unlabelled position by four questions and chooses the repair, with the engine's reading at depth 16 to check
Teaches the whole repair plan back to a beginner and checks the explanation against the self-check list
sources: Move orders and names: app/public/openings (core.json, ECO D30-D69 names) and python-chess replay of every move sequence [V]

Masters statistics: app/public/masters/stats.json (329,379 games, both players 2500 or more, built 2026-10-29); counts quoted exactly from tree rows: position after 6.Nf3 (297 games: h6 185, Nbd7 82, a6 21, b6 9) and the Exchange Variation after 7.Bd3 (594 games: Nbd7 350, O-O 136, h6 92, Bg4 16) [V]
Engine claims: Stockfish 19 lite, single thread, depth 16, in content/items/lesson-od-l-od-qgd-8.json and this lesson's board claims [V]

Positions replayed from the opening move sequences with python-chess; the lesson positions are reconstructions of standard set-ups, not claims about games played; see the position provenance in the item file
Plan ideas (trades first, the b6 route, the minority attack) are standard textbook ideas [R]; they are labelled [R] or [I] where they appear. docs/lesson-depth-standard.md section 6, row 8

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: which Black piece is the problem here? Pick one. We come back to your answer at the end.

steps.text: **The question.** How does the Queen's Gambit Declined go wrong, and how do you repair it? Usually slowly: the engine drifts by a quarter or half a pawn and nobody notices. A few mistakes lose a pawn at once. You will meet four kinds, see what each costs at depth 16 [V], and learn the repair. At the end you diagnose positions with no labels, then teach the whole thing back.

**Error one: the sleeping bishop.** Black's pawns on d5, e6 and c6 stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop, and with the knight on d7 they hold it in. [I] That is why the Declined is called solid but passive. The repair is not speed: it is choosing a way out (a trade, a break or a new diagonal) before the opponent adds pressure.

steps.text: **Why Repair 1 works, and when it does not.** Each trade removes a white piece that kept Black cramped, and the break ...e5 comes after the pin has gone. [I] Played at once, the same break loses a pawn (next chapter). So the condition is: trade first, break second. [H] My guess, not measured: many club players reverse the order because the break feels active.

steps.caption: REPAIR 2: give the bishop another diagonal. Black has played h6 and White has retreated the bishop to h4. This idea does not trade pieces: it moves the bishop to the long diagonal. Purposes are textbook ideas [R]; the number is an engine claim at depth 16 [V].

line.say: The pawn on b6 gives the bishop a route to b7, so it does not have to find a way round the e6 pawn.
White develops; the bishop on d3 points at h7.
The bishop is out at once and looks along the long diagonal toward g2.
White castles.
Black completes development and keeps the structure flexible.

claims.statement: After the line the engine (depth 16) reads +0.1 for White.

steps.text: **What masters play.** In our master data (329,379 games, both players rated 2,500 or more) at least 297 games reach the position after White's sixth move. Black chose h6 in 185 of them (White won 47, Black won 44, 94 draws), the knight move to d7 in 82, a6 in 21 and b6 in nine. These counts are exact tree rows. They show what strong players choose, not which choice is best: draws dominate, and that is a small sample.

steps.prompt: Predict first. The two boards are the same except for White's rook: on a1 (left) or on c1 (right). Black has played Nbd7 on both and White's bishop is still on g5. Does the jump ...Ne4 work in each?
In your own words: which White piece, on which file, made the knight jump fail? Write the condition, not the move.

steps.text: **Error two: the break that arrives too soon.** The ways out of the Declined are breaks: ...c5, ...e5, ...dxc4. Each has conditions. Count the attackers and defenders of the target, check for a pin in the way, check that your pieces are developed, and look for a tactic that changes the count. [I] When a break fails, the engine does not report a small drift: it reports a pawn or more.

steps.caption: The tempting freeing move ...e5, played from the hook position. Two attackers meet one defender on e5, and the white bishop sits on g5 as well. Count before you press.

line.say: Black pushes the pawn to break the centre.
White takes: the pawn on e5 now attacks the f6 knight.
The knight jumps away and offers a trade.
White trades the bishop that pinned the knight; Black's queen will have to recapture.

claims.statement: After ...e5 two white pieces attack the pawn: the d4 pawn and the f3 knight.
Only one black piece defends it: the knight on d7.
After ...e5 the engine (depth 16) reads at least +1.0 for White.
After four moves White is still at least a pawn ahead by the engine's reading (depth 16).

steps.text: **The Exchange Variation changes the structure.** White has taken on d5, so Black has pawns on c6 and d5 but none on e, and White has pawns on d4 and e3 but none on c. White's usual plan is the minority attack: push the b-pawn so that a trade on c6 leaves Black a weak pawn. The engine thinks the plan is worth a small edge only, about a third of a pawn in the positions shown here [V]; that is one position, not a law.

steps.caption: Why the mistimed break fails [V, depth 16]. Count the target square. After ...c5 the pawn on c5 is attacked twice, by the pawns on b4 and d4, and defended once, by the bishop on e7. White simply takes it.

line.say: Black tries the central break at once.
White takes the pawn. Black cannot take back: Bxc5 dxc5 would lose a piece for a pawn.

steps.text: **Why the break fails, and the condition.** Count the target of the break first. ...c5 puts a pawn on c5, which two pawns attack and only the bishop defends, so White wins a pawn at once [V]. The condition for a break: the target has at least as many defenders as attackers, or a tactic behind it changes the count. [I] A break also thins the chain behind it, so check what the moved pawn used to guard.

steps.caption: A second Black slip, after b4, ...a6 and a4. The knights on f8 and f6 both guard h7, and White's queen on c2 stands behind the bishop on d3 along the same diagonal, so a king cannot take on h7. When one guard leaves and the other is traded, the pawn falls. Count the guards before and after.

line.say: The knight leaves f8 to head for the centre.
White trades the bishop for the knight that guarded h7 and d5.
Black recaptures.
White wins a pawn with check: h7 had only the king to defend it, and the queen behind the bishop makes Kxh7 illegal.

claims.statement: After ...Ne6 Bxf6 Bxf6 the engine (depth 16) reads at least +0.9 for White.
At that point the bishop on d3 attacks h7, with the queen on c2 behind it.
Only the king defends the pawn on h7.
A white bishop stands on h7 at the end.
After Bxh7+ the king has two moves (Kh8, Kf8) because it cannot take the bishop.

steps.text: **Errors of White.** White goes wrong in two ways. One is attacking without a target: pushing the h-pawn when there is nothing to hit. The other is greed. The first appears in the Exchange structure, where the h-pawn left alone can become the loose piece. The second is an old trap with a pawn on d5. In both, the engine tells you the cost at once, because the mistake leaves a piece or pawn loose. [V depth 16]

steps.caption: White's lunge h4 in the Exchange structure. It starts an attack with no target. After Black's reply the pawn on h4 has no defender and the kingside is loose; the engine reads Black better [V depth 16].

The knight steps to h5, a square where it is safe, and a trade on e7 is coming.
White trades the bishop that was already attacked.

steps.text: **Diagnosis first.** When a QGD position goes wrong ask four questions in order. Which piece is shut in? Which break is next, and how many attackers does it have? Which defender is overworked? Which of my pawn moves has no target? [I] These four questions correspond to the four errors of this lesson. They are a checklist, not a law: an engine move can break any of them.

Self-check: Did I say when each repair works? When it fails? Give one example a beginner could set up on a board? Name one mistake and its repair?

fields.label: The idea of a repair in this opening:

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
1. Count the moves of the c8 bishop; trade first, break second.
2. Before a break, count attackers and defenders of its target and look for a tactic that changes the count.
3. Do not move a defender that guards two things.
4. Do not push a pawn without a target.
5. In the positions shown, slow errors cost about a third of a pawn and breaks and greed cost a pawn or more. [I]
